recent.impact: None unless a Vaadin 24 application declares observability-kit-starter and whoever can send a baggage header can reach it. There it is a denial of service through memory and CPU, not a way in.
recent.workaround: With Spring Boot, set <opentelemetry.version>1.62.0</opentelemetry.version> in your pom; take it out once your Spring Boot pins 1.62.0 or later. Without Spring Boot that property moves nothing, because only Spring Boot's dependency management reads it: import io.opentelemetry:opentelemetry-bom 1.62.0 in dependencyManagement. Do not declare observability-kit-starter 3.2.1 yourself on 24.4 or 24.7: since 3.2.0 its license listener extends a Flow class that first ships in flow-server 24.9, the listener is a registered service init listener, and the application fails at startup with NoClassDefFoundError. In every case resolution was measured, not compatibility with Observability Kit. If you do not use baggage, otel.propagators=tracecontext drops the baggage propagator instead. These moves change the jar your application resolves and not the copy inside the Observability Kit agent, which carries its own: the 3.2.1 and 4.1.2 agents carry OpenTelemetry 1.62.0 and 1.65.0, both past this one, and the 3.0.0 and 3.1.0 agents carry 1.23.0 and 1.44.1, which are not.
recent.fix_expected: With Spring Boot, on 24.4 and 24.7 none from any Spring Boot you can download: Maven Central ends those lines at 3.2.12 and 3.4.13, which pin 1.31.0 and 1.43.0, and later releases are published by Broadcom under commercial Spring support. On 24.9 and 24.10 a Spring Boot 3.5 patch pinning 1.62.0, which does not exist yet: 3.5.16, the newest open one, pins 1.49.0. Without Spring Boot, 24.9 and 24.10 already resolve 1.62.0 through Observability Kit 3.2.1 and need nothing, and on 24.4 and 24.7 the exit is an Observability Kit release built for those lines, a 3.1.1 from the 3.1.0 tag carrying a fixed OpenTelemetry, and a platform release pinning it on both branches. Kit 3.2.1 and later cannot be that release: they fail at startup on any Flow before 24.9.
recent.commentary: OpenTelemetry reaches a deployed Vaadin 24 application only through Observability Kit; TestBench brings the same jar at test scope. An oversized W3C baggage header makes the parser allocate without a bound, and baggage propagation is on by default. Which release decides the version depends on the shape of the application. With Spring Boot its dependency management pins 1.31.0 on 24.4, 1.43.0 on 24.7 and 1.49.0 on 24.9 and 24.10, all affected. Without Spring Boot the version is the one the Observability Kit the platform pins carries: 1.23.0 on 24.4 through kit 3.0.0 and 1.44.1 on 24.7 through kit 3.1.0, both affected, while 24.9 and 24.10 pin kit 3.2.1, which carries 1.62.0, so that shape is already past it. The 25 series resolve 1.62.0, which is fixed.

recent.impact: None unless the application runs an Observability Kit agent older than 3.2.2, or code of its own extracts trace context from incoming requests. There anybody who can send a request can make each one cost CPU through a crafted tracestate header, a denial of service and not a way in.
recent.workaround: Update the agent to observability-kit-agent 3.2.2 from Maven Central; it is the jar the JVM is started with, so no application rebuild is involved. Until then, cap or remove the tracestate header at your proxy or load balancer before requests reach the application, or start the agent with -Dotel.propagators=none if you do not need trace context from upstream callers. Raising opentelemetry.version in your pom moves the jar your scanner reports and does not change the agent.
recent.fix_expected: The observability-kit-agent 3.2.2 on Maven Central, published on 2026-11-11, built on the upstream Java agent 2.33.1, whose shaded parser scans the header instead of compiling a pattern for it.
recent.commentary: The copy that matters is not the one your scanner found. OpenTelemetry reaches a deployed Vaadin 24 application through Observability Kit, and Observability Kit 3 works through a Java agent that carries its own OpenTelemetry inside it. That agent extracts the W3C trace context of every incoming request with the tracestate parser this advisory describes: a long run of spaces or tabs costs CPU that grows with the square of its length. Agents up to 3.2.1 carry it, because the parser comes from the upstream Java agent the kit is built on rather than from the OpenTelemetry version it declares; the 3.2.2 agent, published on 2026-11-11, carries the rewritten parser, so what remains exposed is an agent older than that. The opentelemetry-api jar your scanner reports is a different copy, and nothing in a Vaadin application passes it an incoming header unless your own code does. Without Observability Kit that jar arrives only through TestBench, which parses no incoming header.

recent.impact: None in a deployed application: it carries no Jackson. On the build machine all four need a hostile JSON document to reach the parser, and a widgetset build parses JSON from nowhere.
recent.commentary: The Jackson your scanner found is on the classpath of the widgetset plugin and the application you deploy carries none: Vaadin 7 and 8 are servlet applications with no JSON binding in them. vaadin-maven-plugin declares resteasy-client and resteasy-jackson2-provider 6.2.11.Final directly, which is what brings jackson-core 2.18.1. All four advisories are denials of service on a crafted document: a number token of unbounded length that the async parser fails to constrain, quadratic backtracking in the float pattern of looksLikeValidNumber, and two more of that family. Every one of them needs the build to parse JSON somebody hostile wrote. The only goal here that makes an HTTP request at all is the widgetset compilation when you ask it for the CDN mode, and the client it drives is compiled against javax.ws.rs while every Jackson provider on this classpath implements jakarta.ws.rs, so they cannot serve its response. Everything else the build reads is your own project. The war you deploy resolves no Jackson on any path.

recent.impact: None in a deployed application: it carries no Jackson. On the build machine every one of the thirteen needs JSON from somebody hostile to be bound onto a class, and the widgetset build binds none.
recent.commentary: The Jackson data binding your scanner found is on the classpath of the widgetset plugin and the application you deploy carries none: Vaadin 7 and 8 are servlet applications with no JSON binding in them. vaadin-maven-plugin declares resteasy-jackson2-provider 6.2.11.Final directly, which is what brings jackson-databind 2.18.1. The thirteen are of two kinds and neither one happens here. Most are bypasses of an annotation that was supposed to keep a field out, @JsonView, @JsonIgnore or a type id on a creator property, which need an application that binds JSON from an outside party onto its own annotated classes. The rest are denials of service on a crafted document. The build binds no JSON to anything: the only goal that speaks to a server is the widgetset compilation in CDN mode, whose client is compiled against javax.ws.rs while every Jackson provider here implements jakarta.ws.rs. The war you deploy resolves no Jackson on any path.

recent.impact: None in a deployed application: it carries no BeanUtils. On the build machine the bypass needs something to pass property names somebody hostile wrote into PropertyUtils, and the only holders of that class here are the Maven site rendering chain, which a widgetset build never invokes.
recent.commentary: The BeanUtils your scanner found rides in on the Maven site rendering stack of the widgetset plugin, and the application you deploy carries none. vaadin-maven-plugin depends on maven-reporting-impl for its report goals, which brings doxia-site-renderer 2.0.0 and under it velocity-tools-generic 3.1, which is what declares commons-beanutils 1.9.4. The advisory is an access control bypass: when an application lets an outside party choose which bean property to read or write, the declared class property of an enum opens a route to the classloader, and 1.9.2 added the BeanIntrospector that stops it without turning it on by default. A widgetset compilation renders no site and maps no property names from anywhere but your own project files. The war you deploy resolves no BeanUtils on any path.

recent.impact: None in a deployed application: it carries no JUnit. On a build machine the exposure needs another untrusted local user on the same host while tests using TemporaryFolder run, and the JUnit your tests actually run with is the one your own pom declares.
recent.commentary: The JUnit your scanner found rides on the classpath of the plugin that builds the widgetset on Vaadin 7, and the application you deploy carries none. The advisory is about the TemporaryFolder test rule: on unix-like systems it creates its directory under /tmp with permissions that let other local users on the same machine read what the tests write there. The plugin declares junit 4.11 as an ordinary dependency and never runs your tests; the tests of your own project run with whatever JUnit your own pom declares, which is the copy to move past 4.13.1 if your builds share a machine with untrusted local users. On Vaadin 8 the same plugin already carries 4.13.2, past the fix. The war you deploy resolves no JUnit on any path.

recent.impact: None in a deployed application: it carries no commons-compress. On the build machine the three need the build to read an archive somebody hostile produced, which means controlling your artifact repository or your source tree.
recent.commentary: The commons-compress your scanner found is on your build machine and the application you deploy carries none. On Vaadin 7 and 8 the plugin that builds the widgetset resolves commons-compress 1.23.0 through plexus-archiver, the library Maven plugins use to pack and unpack archives. The three advisories are all about reading a crafted archive: a TAR whose PAX header is broken, a Pack200 file that exhausts memory, and a DUMP file that loops. What the build packs and unpacks are the archives of your own project and the artifacts your configured repositories serve, not anything a user of the application sends. The war you deploy resolves no commons-compress on any path.

recent.impact: None in a deployed application: it carries no Commons Lang. On the build machine the overflow needs a class name thousands of characters long to reach ClassUtils.getClass, which on Vaadin 7 has no caller here at all and on Vaadin 8 has one, in the site rendering stack the widgetset build never runs.
recent.commentary: The Commons Lang your scanner found is on your build machine and the application you deploy carries none. vaadin-maven-plugin declares commons-lang3 3.17.0 directly. The advisory is uncontrolled recursion: ClassUtils.getClass parses a class name recursively, so a name thousands of characters long throws a StackOverflowError, which an application does not catch. On the Vaadin 7 classpath no class outside commons-lang3 itself names ClassUtils at all. On the Vaadin 8 one there is a single caller, ConstantStringLookup of commons-text 1.12.0, which resolves a const: lookup during string interpolation and belongs to the Maven site rendering chain under maven-reporting-impl; a widgetset compilation renders no site, and the class name it would be handed comes from the document being interpolated rather than from anywhere else. The war you deploy resolves no commons-lang3 on any path.

recent.impact: None in a deployed application: it carries no maven-core. On the build machine the resolution behaviour the advisory describes belongs to the Maven you run, so a build run with Maven 3.8.1 or later is not exposed whatever this plugin carries.
recent.commentary: The maven-core your scanner found is a library on the classpath of the plugin that builds the widgetset on Vaadin 7 and 8, not the Maven that runs your build, and the application you deploy carries none. The advisory is about how Maven itself resolves dependencies: before Maven 3.8.1 it follows custom repository URLs declared in dependency poms, including plain HTTP ones a network attacker can tamper with. That resolution is done by the Maven installation you run, so whether you are exposed is decided by its version, not by this jar: the plugin carries maven-core 3.1.0 on Vaadin 7 and 2.0.6 on Vaadin 8 only as the API that maven-archiver and the reporting machinery link against, and it resolves nothing. Running your builds with Maven 3.8.1 or later is what closes the advisory, and the war you deploy resolves no maven-core on any path.

recent.impact: None in a deployed application: it carries none. On the build machine the traversal needs something to call Expand.extractFile on an archive somebody hostile wrote, and no class of the widgetset build calls it at all.
recent.commentary: The plexus-utils your scanner found is on your build machine and the application you deploy carries none. vaadin-maven-plugin, the plugin that compiles the widgetset on Vaadin 7 and 8, declares plexus-utils 4.0.2 directly and excludes the one maven-archiver would have brought. The advisory is a directory traversal in Expand.extractFile, which unpacks an archive and can write outside the target directory, and nothing on this classpath calls Expand: the only other holders of the name are the copies surefire shades under its own package, which are a different coordinate and not what the scanner reports. The war you deploy resolves no plexus-utils on any path. This is the same answer the 14, 23, 24 and 25 lines already carry for this advisory, measured again on this classpath.

recent.impact: None in a deployed application: it carries no FreeMarker. On the build machine the traversal needs a malformed locale identifier from somebody hostile and a template loader that can reach the file they are after, and the only goal that loads a template reads templates out of the plugin jar under the JVM locale.
recent.commentary: The FreeMarker your scanner found belongs to a goal you run by hand in your IDE setup, and the application you deploy carries none. vaadin-maven-plugin declares freemarker 2.3.20 directly, and the only classes that touch it are EclipseMojo and EclipseTestMojo, the gwt:eclipse goals that write Eclipse launch configurations from templates shipped inside the plugin jar. A widgetset compilation never runs them. The advisory is a path traversal through the localized template lookup, which needs an attacker to name an arbitrary malformed locale identifier, and the lookup here is bounded twice over: the configuration loads templates with setClassForTemplateLoading, so the loader can only reach resources of the plugin jar itself, and the locale is the one the JVM is running under rather than anything an outside party chooses. The war you deploy resolves no FreeMarker on any path.

recent.impact: None in a deployed application: it carries no Snappy. On the build machine the crash needs the build to decompress data somebody hostile produced, and what it would crash is the build, not the application.
recent.commentary: The Snappy your scanner found is on your build machine and the application you deploy carries none. On Vaadin 7 and 8 the plugin that builds the widgetset resolves org.iq80.snappy 0.4 through plexus-archiver, the library Maven plugins use to pack and unpack archives, where it decompresses Snappy streams. The advisory is an out of bounds read while uncompressing crafted data, which crashes the JVM doing the uncompressing. The data the build decompresses comes from the archives of your own project and the artifacts your configured repositories serve, not from anything a user of the application sends. The war you deploy resolves no Snappy on any path.
